title: Port Wine Hangover: Why Fortified Wine Hits So Hard
excerpt: Why port, sherry and vermouth can leave you with a rough morning: the real alcohol content, the role of sugar and congeners, standard-drink math, and how to enjoy them without the hangover.
metaDescription: Why port and other fortified wines cause bad hangovers: higher alcohol, hidden sweetness, late-night timing. Plus sherry and vermouth, and how to avoid it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The answer first:** port gives people bad hangovers mainly because it's strong and easy to drink. Port is usually around 19 to 22% alcohol, roughly one and a half times as strong as an ordinary glass of red wine. It's sweet, which hides that strength. And it's almost always drunk at the end of the evening, after cocktails and a bottle of wine have already been shared around the table. Sherry, Madeira, Marsala and vermouth are in the same family of fortified wines, and they work the same way. The good news is that this makes a fortified-wine hangover fairly predictable, and fairly avoidable.

This guide explains what fortified wine actually is, why port in particular has such a reputation, how sherry and vermouth compare, and what you can do before, during and after a glass or two to make the next morning easier.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is unpleasant but passes within a day. Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, has blue or pale skin, or is vomiting and can't keep anything down. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. See a doctor soon if you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, have severe stomach or chest pain, notice your heart racing or skipping for hours, or feel shaky, sweaty and anxious every time you stop drinking. Those last symptoms can be alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue worth taking seriously and talking to a doctor about, not something to push through.

## What Is Fortified Wine?

A fortified wine is a wine that has had a distilled grape spirit (essentially an unaged brandy) added to it. The extra spirit raises the alcohol level well above that of ordinary table wine, and it was originally done to help wine survive long sea voyages without spoiling.

The timing of when the spirit is added decides whether the wine ends up sweet or dry:

- **Added during fermentation**, the spirit stops the yeast before it has turned all the grape sugar into alcohol. The wine keeps a lot of natural sweetness. This is how port is made.
- **Added after fermentation**, the wine has already used up its sugar, so it stays dry. This is how dry sherries such as fino are made. Sweet sherries are often sweetened afterwards or made from dried, very sugary grapes.

Here is how the common fortified wines compare. Alcohol levels vary by producer and style, so treat these as typical ranges, not exact figures.

| Drink | Typical alcohol | Sweetness | How it's usually served |
|---|---|---|---|
| Red table wine (for comparison) | 12 to 15% | Usually dry | 5 oz glass |
| Ruby or tawny port | 19 to 22% | Sweet | 2 to 3 oz after dinner |
| Fino or manzanilla sherry | About 15% | Bone dry | Small glass, chilled, with food |
| Oloroso sherry | 17 to 20% | Dry or sweetened | Small glass |
| Pedro Ximenez (PX) sherry | 15 to 22% | Very sweet | Small glass with dessert |
| Madeira | 17 to 22% | Dry to sweet | Small glass |
| Marsala | 15 to 20% | Dry to sweet | Often used in cooking, sometimes sipped |
| Vermouth | 15 to 18% | Dry or sweet | Mostly in cocktails |

The pattern that matters for your morning is simple: **every one of these is stronger than table wine, and some are close to half the strength of vodka.**

## Why Port Gives You a Worse Hangover

There isn't one magic ingredient in port that causes hangovers. Instead, several ordinary factors stack up in the same glass. Here they are, roughly in order of how much they matter.

### 1. The alcohol dose is bigger than it looks

This is the main reason, and it's the one people underestimate. In the US, one standard drink is 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's about 5 ounces of 12% table wine, or about 3 ounces of 20% port.

So a proper port pour of 2 to 3 ounces is about one drink. But port is often served generously at home, in a regular wine glass, and topped up. A 6 ounce glass of port is roughly two standard drinks. Three of those after dinner is about six drinks, before you count anything you had earlier in the evening.

How bad a hangover gets depends mostly on how much alcohol you drank. Research reviews on hangovers, including work by the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, have consistently found that the amount of alcohol is the strongest predictor of how bad the next day feels. Port simply delivers that alcohol faster per sip.

### 2. Sweetness hides the strength

Port tastes like a rich, sweet red wine. The sugar softens the burn that would normally warn you that you're drinking something strong. Most people would never drink three big glasses of brandy after dinner, but three glasses of port feels like a gentle way to finish the meal, even though it can add up to a similar amount of alcohol.

There is no good evidence that sugar itself makes hangovers worse. Our guide on [whether sugar helps or hurts a hangover](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover) goes into this. The issue with sweet drinks is that they make it easy to drink more than you intended.

### 3. It comes last, on top of everything else

Port and other dessert wines are usually the final drink of a long evening. By the time the port comes out, many people have already had an aperitif and several glasses of wine. The port is not replacing those drinks. It's being added to them.

That timing hurts in two ways. It pushes your total alcohol for the night higher, and it means you go to bed with more alcohol still in your system. Alcohol can help you fall asleep, but it disrupts sleep later in the night, so you wake up more tired. Many people blame "the port" for a hangover that really came from the whole evening, with the port as the final push.

### 4. Dark, aged drinks carry more congeners

Congeners are the by-products that form during fermentation and ageing, such as methanol, other alcohols, and various flavor compounds. Darker drinks generally contain more of them than clear ones. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, found that people who drank bourbon reported worse hangovers than people who drank the same amount of vodka, which has very few congeners.

Port is a dark red wine, and many ports spend years in wooden barrels, so it's reasonable to expect it to sit on the higher-congener side. No one has run a study comparing port hangovers directly to other drinks, though, so this is an educated guess, not a measured fact. The effect of congeners in research has also been smaller than the effect of the alcohol dose itself. Our article on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains how they work.

### 5. Red-wine compounds, for some people

Ruby and tawny ports are made from red grapes, so they carry the same compounds that make some people sensitive to red wine. Red wines contain more histamine and tannins than whites, and a 2023 study from researchers at UC Davis suggested that quercetin, a compound in grape skins, might interfere with how the body clears alcohol in some people, leading to headaches. That idea is still being tested and hasn't been confirmed in people.

If ordinary red wine reliably gives you a headache within an hour or so, port may do the same. See our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) for more on what is and isn't known.

### What about sulfites?

Sulfites get blamed for a lot of wine headaches, but the evidence doesn't support them as a common cause. Many dried fruits contain more sulfites than wine does. A small number of people, mainly some with asthma, do react to sulfites, usually with breathing symptoms rather than a headache the next day. Our [sulfites and wine headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) article covers this in detail.

## Sherry Hangovers: Why They're Usually Milder

Sherry has a fussy, old-fashioned image, but as hangover risks go it's often one of the gentler fortified wines, for a few reasons.

- **Dry sherries are only a little stronger than table wine.** Fino and manzanilla usually sit around 15% alcohol, not far above a big red wine.
- **They have almost no sugar.** Dry sherry tastes sharp and salty, so you notice what you're drinking and tend to sip it slowly.
- **It's usually served in small glasses with food.** In Spain, a glass of fino comes with olives, almonds, ham or seafood. Eating while you drink slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream.

There is one quirk worth knowing. Fino and manzanilla are aged under a layer of yeast called flor, and that yeast produces acetaldehyde, which gives these sherries their nutty, bruised-apple smell. Acetaldehyde is also the toxic compound your body makes when it breaks down alcohol, and it's one of the suspects behind hangover symptoms. However, the amount you get from your own liver breaking down the alcohol is far larger than what's in the glass, so there is no good evidence that the acetaldehyde in sherry makes a meaningful difference to how you feel the next day.

The sherries that do behave more like port are the **sweet and strong ones**: cream sherries, oloroso sweetened for dessert, and Pedro Ximenez. They can reach 17 to 22% alcohol and have a lot of sugar, which brings back the same "easy to drink too much" problem.

If you have a sherry hangover, the most likely reason is the same as with port: too many glasses, often on top of wine.

## Vermouth Hangovers: Usually It's the Cocktail

Vermouth is a fortified wine flavored with herbs, roots, bark and spices. Dry (often called French) vermouth and sweet (often called Italian) vermouth both usually land between 15 and 18% alcohol.

On its own, vermouth is actually a fairly moderate drink. A 3 ounce pour over ice with a slice of orange is about one standard drink or a little less. Vermouth on the rocks or as a spritz with soda water is one of the lower-alcohol ways to have an aperitif.

The trouble is that most vermouth people drink arrives inside a cocktail:

- **Manhattan:** whiskey with sweet vermouth.
- **Martini:** gin or vodka with a splash of dry vermouth.
- **Negroni:** equal parts gin, Campari and sweet vermouth.

In each of these, most of the alcohol comes from the spirit. A generously made Manhattan or Negroni can contain close to two standard drinks, and because they're stirred and served cold, they go down quickly. If you wake up rough after a night of Negronis, the vermouth is a minor player.

One more point: vermouth is meant to be kept in the fridge after opening and used within a few weeks. Old, oxidized vermouth tastes flat and stale, but there's no evidence it gives you a worse hangover. It's simply less pleasant to drink.

## Madeira and Marsala

Madeira and Marsala get less attention, but the same logic applies. Madeira is often 17 to 22% alcohol and is famously heated and oxidized during ageing, which makes it extremely stable once opened. Marsala is used more in cooking than for sipping, and cooking burns off some, though not all, of the alcohol. As drinks, both behave much like port or sherry of similar strength and sweetness: the stronger and sweeter the style, and the bigger the pour, the more likely you are to feel it the next day.

## How to Enjoy Port Without the Morning After

You don't need to give up port to avoid the hangover. A few simple habits make a big difference, and they all come back to controlling the alcohol dose.

### Before and during

1. **Use a small glass.** A proper port or sherry glass holds about 2 to 3 ounces. If you only have wine glasses, pour about a third of what you'd pour for table wine.
2. **Treat it as a replacement, not an extra.** If you know port is coming at the end of dinner, slow down on the wine during the meal or skip the last glass.
3. **Count it honestly.** One small glass of port is roughly one drink. One big glass is roughly two.
4. **Drink water alongside it.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and helps with the dry mouth and thirst that alcohol causes. Our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
5. **Eat.** Port pairs well with cheese, nuts and chocolate. Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption, though it won't cancel out a large amount of alcohol.
6. **Stop earlier in the night.** Ending the drinking an hour or two before bed gives your body more time to clear alcohol before you sleep. On average, the body clears about one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot between people.

### The next morning

If you do overdo it, the basics are the same as for any hangover:

- **Rehydrate.** Water, and an electrolyte drink if you've been vomiting or feel very dry.
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, eggs, bananas or soup. Bland carbohydrates can help if your blood sugar feels low.
- **Rest.** Sleep is the one thing that reliably helps, because only time actually clears a hangover.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that's already upset from alcohol, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) adds work for your liver. If you use one, take a single label dose with food. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the risks in more detail.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** A glass of port the next morning just delays the hangover and adds to the alcohol your body has to deal with.

For a fuller look at the morning after wine of any kind, see our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide).

## Is It the Port, or Is It You?

It's worth looking honestly at the pattern. If you get a bad hangover after even one small glass of port or sherry, something other than the alcohol dose may be going on. Some possibilities to consider:

- **Red wine sensitivity.** If red wine gives you a headache too, the shared compounds in red grapes may be the culprit. Try a white port or a dry sherry and see if you react differently.
- **Migraine triggers.** Alcohol, especially red wine, is a common migraine trigger. If your "hangover" headache is one-sided, throbbing and comes with light sensitivity or nausea, it may be a migraine, and a doctor can help with that.
- **Medications.** Some medicines interact with alcohol and can make you feel much worse after a small amount, including certain antibiotics, antidepressants, sleep aids and blood pressure medicines. If you're on any regular medication, ask a pharmacist whether alcohol is a problem with it.
- **Flushing.** If your face turns red and hot quickly after a drink, you may have a reduced ability to break down acetaldehyde, which is common in people of East Asian descent. Strong drinks like port can make that worse.

If small amounts consistently make you feel ill, it's worth mentioning to your doctor rather than just avoiding the drink.

## A Note on Supplements

Some people take supplements before or after a night out, and the most-searched one is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the research on DHM comes from animal and lab studies on alcohol metabolism and the liver, with only limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it can prevent a hangover from a heavy night of port.

If you want to try it as part of a sensible plan (smaller pours, water, food and stopping earlier), a well-reviewed option is [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), or the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. No supplement replaces the basic rule: the less alcohol you drink, the better you'll feel.

## The Bottom Line

- Fortified wines such as port, sherry, Madeira, Marsala and vermouth have grape spirit added, which makes them stronger than table wine, usually 15 to 22% alcohol.
- Port hangovers are mostly about dose. It's strong, sweet enough to hide that strength, often poured too big, and drunk at the end of a long night.
- Darker, aged ports likely carry more congeners, and red-grape compounds may bother some people, but these matter less than how much you drank.
- Dry sherry is usually gentler: a bit stronger than wine, no sugar, small glasses and food. Sweet sherries behave more like port.
- Vermouth on its own is moderate. A vermouth "hangover" is usually a cocktail hangover from the gin or whiskey it was mixed with.
- Small glasses, water, food and stopping earlier are what actually work.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked). If sweet wines in general give you a headache, our [sweet wine headache guide](/never-hungover/sweet-wine-headache) covers why.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does port give you such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because of the alcohol dose. Port is usually around 19 to 22% alcohol, roughly one and a half times as strong as table wine, and a full wine glass of it holds close to two standard drinks. It's also sweet, so the alcohol is easy to miss, it tends to be drunk at the end of a night on top of other drinks, and as a dark, wood-aged red it carries more congeners (by-products of fermentation and ageing) than clear drinks. Any one of those makes a rough morning more likely, and port usually brings all of them at once.

**Is a port hangover worse than a regular wine hangover?**

Glass for glass, usually yes, because each glass of port has much more alcohol in it. Drink for drink, measured in standard drinks, there is no good evidence that port is dramatically worse than red table wine. The difference people notice comes mostly from pour size, the late-night timing, and the fact that port is drunk after wine rather than instead of it.

**Does sherry give you a hangover?**

It can, like any alcoholic drink. Dry sherries such as fino and manzanilla are around 15% alcohol, a little stronger than most table wine, while oloroso and sweet sherries such as Pedro Ximenez can reach 17 to 22%. Sherry is traditionally served in small glasses, which helps. Dry styles have almost no sugar, so if you get a bad sherry hangover it's usually down to how many glasses you had and what you drank before and after.

**Does vermouth cause hangovers?**

Vermouth is a fortified wine flavored with herbs and spices, usually around 15 to 18% alcohol. On its own, served in a small pour, it's lower in alcohol than most cocktails. The bigger issue is that vermouth usually arrives inside a Manhattan, martini or Negroni, where it's mixed with gin, whiskey or Campari. In those drinks the spirit is doing most of the damage, and a single cocktail can hold close to two standard drinks.

**How much port is one standard drink?**

In the US, a standard drink is 14 grams of alcohol, which works out to about 3 ounces (roughly 90 ml) of a fortified wine at 20% alcohol. A typical restaurant pour of port is 2 to 3 ounces, so it's close to one drink. A full 5 to 6 ounce wine glass filled with port is closer to two.

**Does the sugar in port make the hangover worse?**

There is no good evidence that sugar itself makes a hangover worse. The more likely problem is indirect: sweetness hides the strength of the alcohol, so it's easy to drink more than you meant to. Sugar can also leave you with a sticky mouth and an upset stomach if you drink a lot of it late at night, but the alcohol dose is still the main driver.

**Are tawny ports or ruby ports worse for hangovers?**

Nobody has studied this directly, so any confident answer is a guess. Both are fortified to similar strength. Tawny ports spend longer in wood and are deliberately oxidized, which changes their flavor compounds, while ruby ports are younger and fruitier. The alcohol level and how much you drink will matter far more than the style.

**Can DHM stop a port hangover?**

There is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement can prevent a hangover from a heavy night of port. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound with early research on alcohol metabolism, mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data. Some people use it alongside sensible habits, but the reliable way to avoid a fortified-wine hangover is smaller pours, fewer glasses and plenty of water.
